title: Precision CRISPR Guide RNA Design for Differentially Expressed Genes in COVID-19
text:
Preface
This report presents our group project for IFN646 Biomedical Data Science at Queensland University of Technology. It connects three stages of a biomedical data analysis: identifying changes in gene expression, selecting CRISPR guide RNAs, and assessing how human genetic variation may affect those guides.
The project uses real biomedical data within a teaching scenario. Its working hypothesis is that regulating genes affected by COVID-19 could support recovery. This hypothesis provides a reason for the analysis; the project does not test whether the proposed guides improve clinical outcomes.
The report follows the decisions from the RNA-seq analysis to the evaluation of OAS2 and the selected guides 200forw and 248forw. Each task explains the approach, presents the findings, and discusses what the results support. The final chapters bring these findings together and document how to reproduce the analysis.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
This report presents a three-stage analysis of biomedical data. The project explores how differential-expression results can support CRISPR guide design in a teaching scenario about COVID-19.
The project uses three statements to frame the analysis:

COVID-19 patients suffer from a deregulation in gene expression.
CRISPR can be used to regulate the expression of specific genes of interest.
Restoring the expression of selected genes could improve recovery. This is the fictional working hypothesis used for the project.

The analysis addresses three tasks. It does not test whether the proposed guides improve recovery:

Differential Expression Analysis: Using raw RNA-seq counts and agreement between two tools to identify genes with different expression in SARS and mock samples.
CRISPR Guide RNA (gRNA) Design: Selecting guides in the first exon of a consensus gene, choosing CRISPRi or CRISPRa based on the expression change, and comparing predicted efficiency and specificity.
Genomic Variation Assessment: Using individual variant information to reassess guide suitability and possible off-target recognition. For the selected CRISPRi strategy, unintended gene regulation is the relevant concern.

title: 2  Task 1: Differential Expression Analysis
text:
2.1 Objective
The first stage of this study aims to identify human genes that are significantly deregulated during SARS-CoV-2 infection compared with uninfected (mock) controls. Because individual differential expression (DE) algorithms rely on different normalisation, dispersion-estimation, and hypothesis-testing assumptions, relying on a single tool can introduce method-specific false positives—especially in small-sample transcriptomic datasets. Task 1 therefore establishes a rigorous preprocessing workflow, evaluates differential expression independently using two complementary statistical frameworks (DESeq2 and edgeR), and applies a conservative consensus strategy to select a high-confidence candidate gene for CRISPR guide design in Task 2.

title: 2  Task 1: Differential Expression Analysis
text:
2.2 Approach

Experimental Design and Metadata Extraction
The raw RNA-seq dataset (gse159717_rnaseq_deseq_5dpi_counts_raw.tsv) comprises 60,683 genomic features across six samples collected at 5 days post-infection (5dpi) from two biological donors (Donor 2 and Donor 3) under three conditions: uninfected control (mock), SARS-CoV-2 infected (SARS), and remdesivir-treated (Rem). Sample metadata were parsed directly from the column headers (S_{donor}_{condition}_{time}_{sample_id}), and mock was set as the reference factor level.


Show analysis code
col_names <- colnames(raw_counts_data[7:12])

col_data <- tibble(row_name = col_names) |>
  separate_wider_delim(
    row_name,
    names = c("prefix", "donor", "condition", "time", "id"),
    delim = "_",
    cols_remove = FALSE
  ) |>
  select(row_name, donor, condition, id) |>
  mutate(
    donor = factor(donor, levels = unique(donor)),
    condition = factor(condition, levels = unique(condition))
  ) |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  column_to_rownames(var = "row_name")

col_data <- col_data |>
  mutate(condition = fct_relevel(condition, "mock"))


Two deliberate modelling choices were made before fitting the statistical models:

Retaining all six samples (mock, SARS, and Rem) during model fitting: Although our biological contrast of interest compares SARS against mock, dropping the two Rem samples prior to model fitting would reduce the residual degrees of freedom from 3 to 1. Retaining all six samples allows both tools to leverage the Rem observations when estimating baseline inter-donor differences and gene-wise dispersion parameters, improving statistical stability before extracting the targeted SARS vs. mock contrast.
Additive paired model design (~ donor + condition): Because each donor was sampled across all conditions, an additive blocking factor for donor was included rather than a simple ~ condition design. Accounting for baseline donor-to-donor transcriptome differences prevents donor variance from inflating the residual error term, thereby increasing statistical power to detect the true condition effect.



Rationale for Selecting DESeq2 and edgeR Over Alternative Algorithms
Several classes of differential expression algorithms exist for RNA-seq data. DESeq2 (Love, Huber, and Anders 2014) and edgeR (Robinson, McCarthy, and Smyth 2009) were specifically selected over alternative frameworks for three methodological reasons:

Discrete Negative Binomial modelling vs. normal-approximation transformations (limma-voom): RNA-seq read counts are discrete, non-negative integers that exhibit strong overdispersion (variance exceeding the mean). While limma-voom models log-counts-per-million using precision weights and linear models, benchmark studies show that voom requires larger sample sizes to reliably estimate empirical Bayes variance weights and can lose power or control of the false discovery rate (FDR) when biological replicates are very small (\(n = 2\) donors per group). In contrast, both DESeq2 and edgeR directly model raw counts using a Negative Binomial Generalized Linear Model (GLM), which is mathematically suited to low-replicate count data.
Parametric empirical Bayes shrinkage vs. non-parametric rank methods (NOIseq, SAMseq, Wilcoxon): Non-parametric permutation or rank-based methods avoid distributional assumptions but lack statistical power at \(n = 2\) per group because the minimum achievable p-value from rank permutations is bounded by sample size. DESeq2 and edgeR overcome the small-sample limitation by borrowing information across all genes via empirical Bayes dispersion shrinkage.
Methodological complementarity between DESeq2 and edgeR: Despite sharing a Negative Binomial GLM foundation, DESeq2 and edgeR differ in their normalisation strategies (median-of-ratios vs. Trimmed Mean of M-values [TMM]), low-count filtering (results() independent filtering vs. filterByExpr()), dispersion shrinkage (local regression/MAP shrinkage vs. weighted likelihood empirical Bayes), and hypothesis tests (Wald test vs. Likelihood Ratio Test [LRT]). Combining them tests whether candidate genes are robust to distinct statistical assumptions.



Pre-Filtering and Tool-Specific Normalisation
Of the 60,683 initial genes, 27,356 genes with zero reads across all six samples were removed first, leaving 33,327 expressed genes. Unexpressed genes contain no information on fold change or dispersion, and removing them reduces computational overhead.
Subsequent pre-filtering and normalisation followed each package’s recommended best practices rather than forcing a single identical pre-filter onto both tools, which could bias one model’s dispersion trend:

DESeq2 workflow: Raw counts were normalised using the median-of-ratios method, which scales counts by sample-specific size factors resistant to a small number of highly expressed viral-response genes. Rather than hard-filtering low-count genes prior to dispersion estimation, DESeq2 retains all expressed genes to model the mean-dispersion trend accurately and applies automated independent filtering at the results() stage, using the mean normalised count as a filter statistic to maximise the number of discoveries at \(\alpha = 0.05\).
edgeR workflow: Because edgeR’s TMM normalisation and dispersion estimation are sensitive to sparse low-count features, filterByExpr() was applied first using the ~ donor + condition design matrix to retain only genes with sufficient counts across biological groups. Library sizes were then recalculated (keep.lib.sizes = FALSE) and normalised via Trimmed Mean of M-values (TMM) to correct for sequencing depth and RNA composition bias. Both workflows operate on raw integer counts rather than length-normalised metrics (TPM or FPKM), preserving the count-variance relationship required by the Negative Binomial distribution.



Show analysis code
design_matrix <- model.matrix(
  design,
  data = col_data
)

y <- DGEList(counts = counts_data, sample = col_data)
keep <- filterByExpr(y, design = design_matrix)
y <- y[keep, , keep.lib.sizes = FALSE]
y <- calcNormFactors(y)




Consensus Strategy Justification
To combine the outputs of DESeq2 and edgeR, each tool’s raw p-values were first adjusted for multiple hypothesis testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (\(\text{FDR} / p_{\text{adj}} < 0.05\)) to control the expected proportion of false discoveries across thousands of simultaneous gene tests.
A strict intersection with directional concordance was chosen over alternative combination methods (such as taking the union of significant genes, or combining p-values via Fisher’s method):

Intersection vs. Union: A union maximises sensitivity (recall) but retains genes that pass significance in only one algorithm due to tool-specific dispersion or filtering artefacts. Because Task 2 requires selecting a single high-confidence gene for therapeutic CRISPR targeting, minimising false positives (high precision/specificity) is far more important than maximising gene count.
Directional concordance (sign(log2FC_DESeq2) == sign(logFC_edgeR)): Requiring identical fold-change signs ensures that both models agree on whether transcription is upregulated or downregulated—a critical requirement because the direction of deregulation directly dictates whether CRISPRi (repression) or CRISPRa (activation) is deployed in Task 2.

title: 2  Task 1: Differential Expression Analysis
text:
2.3 Findings

Exploratory Quality Control and Dispersion Modelling
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on regularised log-transformed (rlog) counts confirmed the necessity of the paired ~ donor + condition design (Figure 2.1). The first principal component (PC1) captures 53% of total transcriptomic variance and primarily separates Donor 2 from Donor 3, demonstrating substantial baseline inter-donor variability that would confound an unpaired analysis.








Figure 2.1: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) of rlog-transformed counts across the six samples, coloured by donor.





The mean-dispersion relationship for DESeq2 (Figure 2.2) and the Biological Coefficient of Variation (BCV) for edgeR (Figure 2.3) follow the expected Negative Binomial behaviour: dispersion is highest among low-count genes and decreases smoothly as mean expression rises. Both plots confirm successful empirical Bayes shrinkage toward the fitted trend, stabilising variance estimates despite the two-donor sample size.








Figure 2.2: Gene-wise, fitted, and final shrunken dispersion estimates in DESeq2.













Figure 2.3: Biological Coefficient of Variation (BCV) relative to average log CPM in edgeR.







Individual Tool Results (SARS vs. mock)
Testing the SARS vs. mock contrast at a Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted threshold of \(0.05\) yielded 68 significant differentially expressed genes in DESeq2 (via the Wald test) and 7 significant genes in edgeR (via the GLM Likelihood Ratio Test).


Show analysis code
# DESeq2 Wald test for SARS vs mock
res_deseq <- results(
  dds,
  contrast = c("condition", "SARS", "mock"),
  alpha = 0.05
)

# edgeR GLM Likelihood Ratio Test for SARS vs mock
fit_edger <- glmFit(y_dispersion, design_matrix)
lrt <- glmLRT(fit_edger, coef = "conditionSARS")




Show analysis code
sig_deseq <- deseq_results |> filter(padj < 0.05)
sig_edger <- edger_results |> filter(FDR < 0.05)

print(paste0("Significant genes: ", nrow(sig_deseq), " found by DESeq2 and ", nrow(sig_edger), " found by edgeR"))


[1] "Significant genes: 68 found by DESeq2 and 7 found by edgeR"


The discrepancy in total hit counts (68 vs. 7) reflects edgeR’s stricter upfront filterByExpr() step and conservative robust dispersion estimation with glmLRT on two replicates, whereas DESeq2’s Wald test is more permissive for genes with near-zero baseline counts in the mock group.


Consensus Differentially Expressed Genes
Intersecting the two significant gene lists and enforcing fold-change sign agreement yielded 6 high-confidence consensus genes (Table 2.1), representing 6 of the 7 edgeR hits (85.7%) and 6 of the 68 DESeq2 hits.


Show analysis code
consensus_table <- sig_deseq |>
  select(
    gene_id,
    fold_change_deseq = log2FoldChange,
    adj_p_value_deseq = padj
  ) |>
  inner_join(
    sig_edger |>
      select(gene_id, fold_change_edger = logFC, adj_p_value_edger = FDR),
    by = "gene_id"
  ) |>
  filter(sign(fold_change_deseq) == sign(fold_change_edger)) |>
  left_join(
    raw_counts_data |> select(1:6),
    by = join_by(gene_id)
  ) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ as.character(signif(.x, 3))))

Among the six consensus hits:

Five genes are strongly upregulated in SARS-CoV-2 infection: OAS2, GPRASP1, AC026801.2, IFI27, and CXCL11.
One gene is downregulated: SERPINB2 (\(\log_2\text{FC} = -1.69\) in DESeq2; \(-1.67\) in edgeR).
Biotype diversity: Five genes (OAS2, GPRASP1, IFI27, SERPINB2, CXCL11) are protein-coding, whereas AC026801.2 is a long non-coding RNA (lncRNA).

title: 2  Task 1: Differential Expression Analysis
text:
2.4 Discussion & Conclusion
While OAS2, GPRASP1, and AC026801.2 exhibit extreme positive \(\log_2\) fold changes (\(\approx 9.9\text{ to }10.9\)), these magnitudes must be interpreted with statistical caution: GPRASP1 and AC026801.2 have zero raw counts in both mock samples, and OAS2 has almost zero baseline expression (0 and 2 counts). Because unshrunken maximum-likelihood fold-change estimates are reported, near-zero denominators inflate the \(\log_2\) ratio. Furthermore, with only two biological donors, these results establish transcriptomic deregulation within this specific experimental cohort rather than a population-wide clinical estimate.
Nevertheless, the consensus intersection confirms that OAS2, IFI27, and CXCL11—hallmark interferon-stimulated innate immune genes—are robustly induced across both statistical models. From this six-gene consensus set (data/consensus_table.rds), OAS2 is carried forward to Task 2 for systematic evaluation as a CRISPR therapeutic target.






Love, Michael I, Wolfgang Huber, and Simon Anders. 2014. “Moderated Estimation of Fold Change and Dispersion for RNA-Seq Data with DESeq2.” Genome Biology 15. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-014-0550-8.


Robinson, Mark D., Davis J. McCarthy, and Gordon K. Smyth. 2009. “<Tt>edgeR</Tt>: A Bioconductor Package for Differential Expression Analysis of Digital Gene Expression Data.” Bioinformatics 26: 139–40. https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btp616.

title: 3  Task 2: gRNA Design for OAS2
text:
3.1 Objective
Building on the six consensus differentially expressed genes identified in Task 1 (Table 2.1), Task 2 selects a single biologically justified target gene, determines the appropriate transcriptional modulation strategy (CRISPRi vs. CRISPRa), extracts the canonical first exon sequence relative to gene transcription, and designs candidate SpCas9 single-guide RNAs (gRNAs) balancing on-target efficiency against off-target specificity.
crumbs: 3  Task 2: gRNA Design for OAS2

title: 3  Task 2: gRNA Design for OAS2
text:
3.2 Approach

Rationale for Selecting OAS2 Over the Other Five Consensus Genes
Rather than selecting a target solely by the largest numerical fold change, all six consensus genes from Task 1 (OAS2, GPRASP1, AC026801.2, IFI27, SERPINB2, and CXCL11) were evaluated against three criteria: protein-coding annotation, statistical robustness across both DE tools, and a direct mechanistic link to SARS-CoV-2 pathogenesis:

Exclusion of AC026801.2 (Biotype): AC026801.2 is a poorly characterised long non-coding RNA (lncRNA). Protein-coding genes with well-annotated transcription start sites (TSS) and established functional pathways are strongly preferred for therapeutic CRISPR modulation.
Exclusion of GPRASP1 (Zero baseline & pathway relevance): GPRASP1 has zero read counts in both mock controls (inflating its \(\log_2\text{FC}\)) and encodes a G-protein-coupled receptor sorting protein without a primary role in coronavirus replication or hyperinflammation.
Exclusion of SERPINB2 (Directionality and modest effect size): SERPINB2 is the only downregulated gene (\(\log_2\text{FC} \approx -1.68\)), which would require CRISPR activation (CRISPRa), and exhibits the smallest absolute fold change among the six candidates.
Selection of OAS2 over IFI27 and CXCL11: While OAS2, IFI27, and CXCL11 are all upregulated interferon-stimulated genes, OAS2 (ENSG00000111335) combines an exceptionally strong, highly significant induction in both tools (Table 3.1) with a direct enzymatic role in the innate antiviral response. OAS2 encodes 2’-5’-oligoadenylate synthetase 2, which senses viral double-stranded RNA and synthesises 2’-5’-oligoadenylates to activate latent endoribonuclease RNase L (Merold et al. 2025). Crucially, sustained OAS2 overexpression in late-stage SARS-CoV-2 infection is implicated in pathological hyperinflammation, tissue damage, and COVID-19-associated cardiac dysfunction (Gao et al. 2023; Hernandez-Ramirez et al. 2026), making its controlled downregulation a biologically coherent test case for the project’s expression-restoration hypothesis.

Choice of CRISPR Modality: Why CRISPRi Instead of CRISPRa or Cas9 Nuclease
The overarching project hypothesis states that restoring deregulated gene expression in COVID-19 toward baseline levels will support patient recovery. Because OAS2 is strongly upregulated in the SARS condition (\(\log_2\text{FC} = 9.90\) in DESeq2, \(10.30\) in edgeR), CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) was selected over CRISPRa (which activates transcription of downregulated genes) and standard wild-type Cas9 nuclease cleavage (which causes permanent, irreversible DNA double-strand breaks and frameshift mutations). CRISPRi pairs a catalytically dead Cas9 (dCas9) with a transcriptional repressor domain such as KRAB to sterically block RNA polymerase II elongation and induce reversible heterochromatin silencing near the transcription start site (TSS) and first exon (Jensen et al. 2021).


Transcript, Strand Directionality, and First-Exon Extraction
Because eukaryotic genes often produce multiple alternatively spliced isoforms with different 5’ start sites, selecting an arbitrary transcript could target an exon that is spliced out in the primary physiological isoform. We therefore queried OAS2 in Ensembl (GRCh38.p14) and selected the MANE Select transcript (ENST00000392583.7) (Morales et al. 2022). MANE (Matched Annotation from NCBI and EMBL-EBI) defines the single, clinically standardised canonical transcript agreed upon by both RefSeq and Ensembl.






Figure 3.1: OAS2 gene view in Ensembl (GRCh38.p14) showing the canonical MANE Select transcript ENST00000392583.7 on the forward strand of chromosome 12.



Paying strict attention to genomic directionality as required by the project specification, OAS2 is transcribed on the forward (+) strand of chromosome 12. Consequently, the first exon relative to the 5’ transcription start site is the most upstream exon (ENSE00002421397.2, out of 10 total exons), spanning chr12:112,978,519–112,978,785 (1-based, 267 bp) (Figure 3.2).

Rationale for Selecting CRISPOR Over Other gRNA Design Tools
Multiple computational tools exist for CRISPR guide design, including CHOPCHOP, E-CRISP, SSC, and CRISPOR (Li et al. 2023; Cui et al. 2018; Concordet and Haeussler 2018). CRISPOR was specifically chosen over these alternatives for three reasons guided by both Task 2 and Task 3 requirements:

Multi-model efficiency consensus vs. single-score tools: Unlike tools that report only a single activity metric, CRISPOR simultaneously computes orthogonal on-target efficiency models—including Doench 2016 (Rule Set 2), Moreno-Mateos, and RuleSet3—allowing cross-validation of predicted guide activity (Concordet and Haeussler 2018).
Position- and nucleotide-aware off-target scoring (MIT and CFD): CRISPOR reports both the MIT specificity score and the Cutting Frequency Determination (CFD) score (Haeussler et al. 2016). Because CFD weights both the position and nucleotide identity of mismatches across the 20-nt protospacer and PAM, it provides a more biologically realistic measure of off-target dCas9 binding affinity than simple mismatch counting.
Direct compatibility with Task 3 VCF screening: Crucially for Task 3, CRISPOR allows exporting the complete table of genome-wide off-target intervals (offtargetsguide.txt) with exact 1-based GRCh38 coordinates, strand orientation, mismatch counts, and 23-bp sequences. Tools that only return summary off-target counts without genomic coordinates cannot be intersected with personal VCF files in Task 3.

The 267 bp OAS2 exon 1 sequence was analysed in CRISPOR using the Homo sapiens GRCh38/hg38 assembly, SpCas9 nuclease, canonical 20bp-NGG PAM setting (Figure 3.3).






Figure 3.3: CRISPOR configuration using the human GRCh38/hg38 reference assembly and 20bp-NGG SpCas9 parameters.

title: 3  Task 2: gRNA Design for OAS2
text:
3.3 Findings

Evaluation of Candidate gRNAs in OAS2 Exon 1
CRISPOR identified all candidate 20-nt protospacers adjacent to a canonical NGG PAM across both strands of OAS2 exon 1 (Figure 3.4).






Figure 3.4: CRISPOR output table displaying candidate gRNAs across the first exon of OAS2, ranked by specificity and efficiency metrics.



To select the optimal guide pair, we applied a multi-tiered filtering strategy:

Zero close-match off-targets (0-0-0 filter): Any guide with predicted off-target sites harbouring 0, 1, or 2 mismatches in the reference genome was immediately excluded, as SpCas9/dCas9 readily tolerates 1–2 mismatches.
High genome-wide specificity (\(\text{MIT} \ge 85\) and \(\text{CFD} \ge 95\)): Guides were required to achieve top-tier specificity across both scoring algorithms to minimise unintended transcriptional repression elsewhere in the genome.
Complementary on-target efficiency across models: Because empirical efficiency algorithms weight sequence features differently, we selected two high-specificity guides—200forw (200/fw) and 248forw (248/fw)—that excel across complementary efficiency predictors (Table 3.2).

Justification of 200forw and 248forw Over Alternative Exon 1 Guides
Comparing 200forw and 248forw against each other and against rejected candidates in Figure 3.4 demonstrates why retaining this pair is optimal:

Strengths of 200forw: Achieves the highest overall MIT specificity score (97) and CFD score (96), alongside strong Doench 2016 (64) and Moreno-Mateos (48) efficiency predictions. Its 52 predicted off-target sites consist of zero 0-, 1-, or 2-mismatch sites, only 4 three-mismatch sites, and 48 four-mismatch sites (0-0-0-4-48).
Strengths of 248forw: Matches 200forw in CFD specificity (96) and total off-target count (52, distributed as 0-0-0-5-47), while achieving an outstanding RuleSet3 efficiency score (89) and solid Doench 2016 score (55).
Why other Exon 1 candidates were rejected: Alternative guides visible in Figure 3.4 are inferior on either specificity or efficiency. For example, 166/rev has lower specificity (MIT 90, CFD 92) and 50% more off-target sites (79 vs. 52), while 150/rev is flagged by CRISPOR as "Inefficient" with a strongly negative RuleSet3 score (-77 vs. 89) and low Doench 2016 score (31).

title: 3  Task 2: gRNA Design for OAS2
text:
3.4 Discussion & Conclusion
Selecting 200forw and 248forw provides a well-balanced pair of forward-strand gRNAs targeting the canonical first exon of OAS2 (chr12:112,978,698–112,978,720 and chr12:112,978,746–112,978,768). Both guides use a canonical TGG PAM, avoid any 0–2 mismatch off-targets in GRCh38, and hedge against single-model bias by combining top-ranked MIT/Doench metrics (200forw) with top-ranked RuleSet3/CFD metrics (248forw).
Two biological caveats apply to these computational predictions. First, CRISPOR’s efficiency scores (Doench 2016, Moreno-Mateos, RuleSet3) were trained primarily on Cas9 knockout cleavage datasets rather than dCas9-KRAB transcriptional repression; while sequence features governing Cas9 ribonucleoprotein assembly and DNA unwinding are shared, steric positioning relative to the TSS also influences CRISPRi efficacy (Jensen et al. 2021; Haeussler et al. 2016). Second, all scores in Task 2 are computed solely against the GRCh38 reference genome. Human genetic polymorphisms can alter on-target availability on chromosome 12 or modify off-target binding risk on other chromosomes. Both 200forw and 248forw, together with their exported CRISPOR off-target coordinates (offtargetsguide.txt), are therefore carried forward to Task 3 for personal genome evaluation across the seven 1000 Genomes individuals.






Concordet, Jean-Paul, and Maximilian Haeussler. 2018. “CRISPOR: Intuitive Guide Selection for CRISPR/Cas9 Genome Editing Experiments and Screens.” Nucleic Acids Research 46 (W1): W242–45. https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gky354.

title: 4  Task 3: Impact of Human Genetic Variation on CRISPR Guide Performance
text:
4.1 Objective
In Task 2, two CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) guides, 200forw and 248forw, were selected to target the first exon of OAS2 on chromosome 12 using CRISPOR predictions (Haeussler et al. 2016). Because human genomes differ from the reference assembly, genetic variation can alter CRISPR guide performance in two ways:
Task 3 evaluates both questions across seven individuals from the 1000 Genomes Project (HG00142, HG00178, HG00237, HG01521, HG03129, NA19175, and NA19462) to refine the guide selection from Task 2.
crumbs: 4  Task 3: Impact of Human Genetic Variation on CRISPR Guide Performance

title: 4  Task 3: Impact of Human Genetic Variation on CRISPR Guide Performance
text:
On-target guide availability: Variants within the target gene may alter the 20-base protospacer or disrupt the 3-base PAM, preventing guide recognition in certain individuals.
Off-target binding risk: Variants within predicted off-target loci across the genome may increase or decrease sequence similarity or alter canonical PAM motifs.
crumbs: 4  Task 3: Impact of Human Genetic Variation on CRISPR Guide Performance

title: 4  Task 3: Impact of Human Genetic Variation on CRISPR Guide Performance
text:
4.2 Approach

Extracting Individual Genotypes from VCF Datasets
Variant Call Format (VCF) files record reference (REF) and alternate (ALT) alleles, genomic coordinates, and phased individual genotypes (0 for the reference allele, 1 for the first alternate allele, separated by | for phased haplotypes) (Danecek et al. 2011). Two complementary VCF sources were used to cover both the intended on-target locus on chromosome 12 and predicted off-target loci on chromosomes 1 and 2:

On-target check (Chromosome 12): Because OAS2 resides on chromosome 12, the GRCh38 phased VCF from the 1000 Genomes Project (ALL.chr12.shapeit2_integrated_snvindels_v2a_27022019.GRCh38.phased.vcf.gz) was subsetted to the OAS2 exon 1 region and the seven target individuals (chr12_OAS2_7samples.vcf). To match the pre-processed chromosome 1 and 2 files, sites where all seven individuals are homozygous for the reference allele (0|0, \(\text{AC} = 0\) in the subset) were filtered out so that only polymorphic variants carried by the seven individuals were retained. The two 23-base target-plus-PAM regions on the forward strand (chr12:112,978,698–112,978,720 for 200forw and chr12:112,978,746–112,978,768 for 248forw) were screened against the Task 2 Ensembl GRCh38 reference sequences.
Off-target check (Chromosomes 1 and 2): The CRISPOR off-target prediction table from Task 2 was filtered for 200forw and 248forw and compared against the provided 7-individual VCF subsets (sampled_chr1.vcf and sampled_chr2.vcf).



Sequence Partitioning and Haplotype Evaluation
In accordance with the SpCas9 recognition mechanism, each 23-base interval was partitioned into its 20-base protospacer and 3-base PAM (canonical NGG) (Haeussler et al. 2016). Mismatches were counted strictly across the 20-base protospacer, while PAM mutations were assessed separately. Using phased genotypes (0|0, 0|1, 1|0, 1|1), both maternal and paternal haplotypes were reconstructed for each individual to distinguish heterozygotes (one altered copy) from alternate homozygotes (two altered copies).
crumbs: 4  Task 3: Impact of Human Genetic Variation on CRISPR Guide Performance

title: 4  Task 3: Impact of Human Genetic Variation on CRISPR Guide Performance
text:
4.3 Findings

On-Target Guide Availability in Individual Genomes (Chromosome 12)
Screening the chromosome 12 OAS2 target intervals across the seven individuals (chr12_OAS2_7samples.vcf) revealed zero polymorphic variants carried by any of the seven individuals in either 200forw or 248forw (Table 4.1). Although four rare population variant records overlap the 248forw protospacer in the full 2,504-person 1000 Genomes release, all seven study individuals carry the homozygous reference genotype (0|0) at every position.

Consequently, both reconstructed chromosome 12 haplotypes in HG00142, HG00178, HG00237, HG01521, HG03129, NA19175, and NA19462 retain zero protospacer mismatches and an intact TGG PAM for both candidate guides. Both 200forw and 248forw remain fully present across all seven genomes.


Variants Affecting Predicted Off-Target Sites (Chromosomes 1 and 2)
Intersecting the CRISPOR-predicted off-target intervals with sampled_chr1.vcf and sampled_chr2.vcf identified one unique variant overlapping a predicted off-target site for guide 248forw, and zero overlapping variants for guide 200forw (Table 4.2, Table 4.3).

Effect on Off-Target Binding Risk
Partitioning the 23-base off-target locus at chr1:224,887,199 shows that the G > A substitution occurs at the third base of the PAM, mutating the canonical AGG PAM to a non-canonical AGA PAM (Table 4.4). The 20-base protospacer is unchanged and remains at 4 mismatches relative to 248forw.

Because SpCas9 strongly prefers a canonical NGG PAM for initial DNA recognition, replacing AGG with AGA reduces the likelihood of off-target dCas9 binding on haplotypes carrying the alternate allele, though low-level recognition at non-canonical NGA PAMs cannot be completely ruled out (Haeussler et al. 2016).
Evaluating phased genotypes reveals distinct individual-level profiles (Table 4.5):

Reference homozygotes (0|0, 3 individuals): HG00178, HG00237, and HG01521 retain the canonical AGG PAM on both chromosome 1 copies.
Heterozygotes (0|1 or 1|0, 3 individuals): HG00142, HG03129, and NA19175 carry the disrupted AGA PAM on one haplotype, but still retain the canonical AGG PAM on their second haplotype.
Alternate homozygote (1|1, 1 individual): NA19462 carries the AGA PAM on both chromosome 1 copies, eliminating the canonical NGG PAM at this locus entirely.

title: 4  Task 3: Impact of Human Genetic Variation on CRISPR Guide Performance
text:
4.4 Discussion
Combining the chromosome 12 on-target analysis with the chromosome 1 and 2 off-target analysis directly refines the Task 2 guide selection across the seven personal genomes:

Both candidate guides remain viable for on-target OAS2 regulation: Neither 200forw nor 248forw is affected by genetic variation in OAS2 exon 1 among the seven individuals. Both guides retain 100% protospacer identity and canonical TGG PAMs on both chromosome 12 haplotypes.
Genotype-specific off-target refinement: Guide 200forw exhibits uniform behaviour across all seven genomes, with no variants intersecting its evaluated off-target intervals. For guide 248forw, the chr1:224,887,199 variant (G > A) does not create a new off-target risk; instead, it disrupts the canonical AGG PAM (AGG \(\rightarrow\) AGA) without reducing the four existing protospacer mismatches. However, because three of the four carriers (HG00142, HG03129, NA19175) are heterozygous, they still retain one functional AGG off-target copy, whereas only NA19462 (1|1) loses the canonical PAM on both chromosomes.
Implications for CRISPRi: Because this therapeutic strategy employs CRISPRi (dCas9 transcriptional repression) rather than nuclease cleavage (Jensen et al. 2021), off-target risk primarily concerns unintended transcriptional silencing if dCas9 binds near a promoter or enhancer, rather than double-stranded DNA breaks. Preserving zero mismatches at the intended OAS2 first exon while maintaining high mismatch counts (4 mismatches) and disrupted PAMs at off-target loci supports the safety and efficacy of both guides.

Two methodological limitations should be noted. First, VCF files report variant calls relative to GRCh38 rather than base-by-base sequencing depth, meaning uncalled regions are assumed to match the reference genome. Second, screening was performed on reference-predicted off-target intervals; personal variants elsewhere in the genome can occasionally generate de novo NGG PAMs that would only be captured by a genome-wide variant-aware search (Lessard et al. 2017).
crumbs: 4  Task 3: Impact of Human Genetic Variation on CRISPR Guide Performance

title: 4  Task 3: Impact of Human Genetic Variation on CRISPR Guide Performance
text:
4.5 Conclusion
Across the seven evaluated 1000 Genomes individuals, chromosome 12 variant screening confirms that both 200forw and 248forw target sites in OAS2 exon 1 are 100% conserved (0|0) on both haplotypes. Off-target screening across chromosomes 1 and 2 identified a single SNP (chr1:224,887,199 G>A) affecting a predicted 248forw off-target site in four individuals, mutating its PAM from AGG to AGA while preserving four protospacer mismatches. Both 200forw and 248forw remain strong candidates for OAS2 CRISPRi modulation, with 200forw showing complete invariance across all assessed loci and 248forw experiencing a haplotype-dependent reduction in canonical PAM availability at one off-target site.
The Reproducibility chapter documents the input files, data access, reproduction workflow and software information. Sources cited here are included in the final References.

title: 5  Summary
text:
Task 1: Consensus Differential Expression Analysis
This project integrates transcriptomic differential expression analysis (Task 1), computational CRISPR guide RNA design (Task 2), and personal genome variant screening (Task 3) into a unified, reproducible R workflow.
To identify genes deregulated during SARS-CoV-2 infection (SARS vs. mock at 5 days post-infection) while controlling for baseline inter-donor variance (~ donor + condition), raw RNA-seq counts were analysed using two complementary Negative Binomial Generalized Linear Model frameworks: DESeq2 (median-of-ratios normalisation, empirical Bayes dispersion shrinkage, and Wald testing) and edgeR (filterByExpr pre-filtering, TMM normalisation, and Likelihood Ratio Testing).
At a Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted threshold of \(0.05\), DESeq2 identified 68 significant genes and edgeR identified 7 significant genes. Applying a conservative intersection with strict fold-change sign concordance yielded six high-confidence consensus genes: five upregulated (OAS2, GPRASP1, AC026801.2, IFI27, and CXCL11) and one downregulated (SERPINB2). Prioritising method intersection over a union or p-value meta-analysis minimised tool-specific false positives prior to downstream guide design.

title: 5  Summary
text:
5.1 Implications and Methodological Limitations








Stage
Key Takeaway
Primary Limitation & Future Direction




Task 1 (Transcriptomics)
Consensus DE modelling (DESeq2 \(\cap\) edgeR) isolates robust interferon-stimulated gene induction (OAS2, IFI27, CXCL11).
Only two biological donors (\(n = 2\)) and near-zero mock counts inflate unshrunken \(\log_2\text{FC}\) magnitudes; validation in larger patient cohorts is required.


Task 2 (gRNA Design)
Pairing 200forw (top MIT/Doench) and 248forw (top RuleSet3/CFD) in OAS2 exon 1 balances specificity and efficiency.
Efficiency models are trained primarily on Cas9 cleavage rather than dCas9-KRAB repression; empirical knockdown assays are needed to confirm steric TSS repression.


Task 3 (Personal Genomes)
Both guides retain 100% on-target conservation on chr12; 200forw is invariant across screened off-targets, while 248forw loses a canonical off-target PAM on ALT alleles.
VCF files do not verify base-level sequencing depth across reference calls, and reference-based off-target lists do not capture de novo variant-created NGG PAMs elsewhere in the genome.

title: 5  Summary
text:
5.2 Overall Conclusion
Across all three analytical stages, 200forw and 248forw emerge as well-supported candidate gRNAs for CRISPRi-mediated modulation of OAS2. Both guides are 100% conserved at their intended chromosome 12 target sites across all seven evaluated human genomes, with 200forw offering the highest genome-wide specificity and complete invariance across screened off-target regions, and 248forw providing a high-efficiency alternative whose single overlapping off-target SNP (chr1:224,887,199 G>A) disrupts a canonical AGG PAM in four carriers. Together, these findings demonstrate how integrating multi-tool transcriptomics with haplotype-aware genomic screening refines precision CRISPR therapeutics prior to experimental validation.

title: 6  Reproducibility
text:
6.1 Project files and data access
The report is organised as a Quarto book. The chapter source files, _quarto.yml, references.bib, the data and figures folders, and renv.lock should be kept together in the Final Report project folder. All R chapters use relative paths so that the project can be moved across machines without relying on machine-specific directory paths.
The group shares the project through its GitHub repository. The Final Report/data folder is the central location for all report inputs and intermediate artefacts. For exact reproduction, retain the repository copy or commit identifier used for rendering.
The following files in Final Report/data are used by the R chapters across Tasks 1, 2, and 3:

title: 6  Reproducibility
text:
6.3 Reproduction workflow
To reproduce the complete report from scratch:

Clone or download the project repository and retain its folder structure.
Open Final Report.Rproj in RStudio in a fresh R session.
Restore the recorded R package environment from renv.lock by running renv::restore().
Render the Quarto book to HTML via the RStudio Render Book button or by running quarto render in the terminal from the Final Report directory.

The three analytical stages execute in sequence during rendering:

Task 1 (Task1.qmd): Reads data/gse159717_rnaseq_deseq_5dpi_counts_raw.tsv, performs the differential expression analyses (DESeq2 and edgeR), and exports the consensus gene table to data/consensus_table.rds.
Task 2 (Task2.qmd): Reads data/consensus_table.rds, justifies the selection of OAS2, extracts the first-exon target region, and evaluates candidate CRISPRi guides (200forw and 248forw) using CRISPOR predictions.
Task 3 (Task3.qmd): Reads data/chr12_OAS2_7samples.vcf to verify on-target guide and PAM conservation across the seven individuals on chromosome 12, and screens data/sampled_chr1.vcf.zip and data/sampled_chr2.vcf.zip against the CRISPOR off-target intervals (data/offtargetsguide.txt / snapshots) to evaluate haplotype-specific off-target binding risk in R.
